sections.h2: Where does Montgomery County, Pennsylvania record a deed?
sections.html:
Deeds for Montgomery County go to the Recorder of Deeds on the third floor of One Montgomery Plaza, 425 Swede Street in Norristown, in Suite 303. Posted hours run weekdays from half past eight until four o'clock, and quick questions can be texted to 267-355-3404.

The county created the office in 1784, the same year it was carved out of Philadelphia County. Its job covers deeds, mortgages, powers of attorney, notary commissions, subdivision and highway plans, and military discharge papers.

For a seller the visit happens last. Papers get signed at the closing table, they travel to Norristown, and the recording date marks the moment the buyer shows up as owner in the public record. That sequence explains why a closing agent keeps asking you for a parcel number.

sections.h2: What does the Montgomery County Recorder of Deeds charge?
sections.html:
Montgomery County starts a deed at $87.75, per the schedule dated November 24, 2025. The price assumes no more than four names, four pages and a single parcel, and every extra is billed on top.

Montgomery County recording charges, schedule effective November 24, 2025
ItemCharge
Deed or mortgage, starting price$87.75
Additional page past the fourth$4.00
Additional name past the fourth$1.00
Additional parcel$15.50
Relocation deed$175.50
Satisfaction of a mortgage$81.75
Document rejection$10.00
Returned check$30.00

Source: the county's Recording Fee Schedule page. A few smaller charges apply too, listed below.

  • Statement of Value forms cost $1.50 for the pair of originals the office wants. A relocation deed needs four originals, at $3.00.
  • Mail a lone document with no return envelope and it costs $2; a bundle costs $10.
  • Cards add a 2.65% convenience charge.
  • Where land sits in two or more taxing authorities, the first unique parcel ID in each one carries a $5.50 fee.

sections.h2: How does Montgomery County collect transfer tax at recording?
sections.html:
The recorder collects it during recording, at a combined 2 percent. One point goes to the state, and under the state's rule the seller and the buyer answer for it jointly.

Montgomery County asks for two separate checks when a deed is recorded: one for the recording fee and one for the realty transfer tax. Payee names the county will honor include "Montco Recorder of Deeds" and "Montgomery County ROD," and each check should print the account holder's address.

Form REV-183, the Statement of Value, rides along whenever the tax is not simply paid on a stated price. Land spread over two or more municipalities calls for a split of value in the deed, so each local tax collector gets the right piece. The fee page also posts a Common Level Ratio Factor, 3.25 as of July 1, 2025 and 3.36 as of July 1, 2026. Ask the office how it applies to a deed that carries no sale price.

Some transfers owe nothing, such as particular gifts inside a family or inherited property. Whether a given family deed qualifies is a question for the closing attorney or the recorder's staff.

sections.h2: Why does a Montgomery County deed stop at the Board of Assessments first?
sections.html:
Montgomery County requires every document, on paper or electronic, to be registered by the Board of Assessments first. The board sits directly across the hall from the recorder on the third floor of One Montgomery Plaza.

Every document also needs a Parcel Identification Number, which is a 12-digit number in this county. If a parcel number appears anywhere on a document, it has to be registered unless the document says in so many words that the number is for reference only. Questions about parcel mapping belong with the Board of Assessments, not the recorder.

Older advice about registering a deed with the township before recording no longer holds. The county rescinded pre-registration on December 9, 2008. Some municipalities still want the deed registered after it is recorded, and the municipality may charge for that. The submitter handles it.

sections.h2: Can a deed be filed online in Montgomery County?
sections.html:
Yes, within limits. The county has taken electronic recordings since fall 2006 and works with Simplifile, the eRecording Partners Network and CSC. Documents usually come back the same day or the next.

The county lists what cannot go through that channel, so a seller's closing agent knows to bring paper.

  • Deeds that contain a trust must be mailed or delivered, because an electronically recorded document becomes public automatically.
  • Mortgages in default, plans and post-construction stormwater documents cannot be submitted electronically.
  • Documents with more than 10 parcels, packages of more than 10 documents and packages above 100 pages are turned away.
  • Scans must be at least 300 DPI, black and white, as TIFF images.

If an electronic filing is rejected and you think the rejection was wrong, the county asks you to call 610-278-3289 the same day so staff can decide whether the rejection fee comes back.

sections.h2: Which errors make Montgomery County return a deed?
sections.html:
Most returns come from small mismatches. The county repeats the Pennsylvania recorders' association standards on its requirements page, and it adds its own.

  • The document must be an original, not a copy.
  • The acknowledgment date cannot be earlier than the document date, and it needs county, state, names, titles, the notary's signature, seal and commission expiration.
  • The number written out must match the numeral on a deed or mortgage.
  • Deeds, mortgages and assignments need a certified grantee or mortgagee address, signed.
  • Blanket documents are refused.
  • Paper submissions need a stamped, self-addressed envelope big enough for the documents.

Each rejection costs $10, so a package that fails twice costs more than one that is checked before it leaves the closing office.

sections.h2: Who is selling in Montgomery County, and where?
sections.html:
Only Philadelphia and Allegheny counties have more people than this suburb of Philadelphia, where Norristown is the seat and Lower Merion Township is the biggest municipality. The 2025 federal estimate is 877,643 residents, and roughly 71 percent of homes are lived in by their owners.

Prices run high: the typical owned home is valued at $436,700 and the typical household earns $113,915, based on the latest five-year survey. Employers cluster around Blue Bell, Lansdale, Fort Washington, Horsham and King of Prussia.

The county is made up of dozens of townships, boroughs and home rule municipalities, and the local share of transfer tax follows whichever one the house sits in. School district names such as Lower Merion, North Penn, Abington and Norristown Area matter when you compare tax bills.

sections.h2: What should be in the closing folder for a Montgomery County sale?
sections.html:
Bring the paperwork that the recorder will otherwise bounce. A few items cause most of the delay.

  • The 12-digit parcel number, checked against the Board of Assessments.
  • Two original Statement of Value forms, fully filled in.
  • Two checks, one for the recording fee and one for transfer tax, each with the account holder's address.
  • A prepaid return envelope if the deed comes back by mail.
  • A plan for any trust deed, since those cannot be filed electronically.

Your title company normally handles all of this. It still helps to ask who is paying the recording fee and the buyer's half of the tax, because the sales contract can shift those costs from the default.

faqs.q: What is the price of recording a Montgomery County deed?
faqs.a: The base fee is $87.75 for up to four names, four pages and one parcel, plus $1 per extra name, $4 per extra page and $15.50 per extra parcel. Transfer tax and a $1.50 Statement of Value fee are separate.

faqs.q: Does Montgomery County take one check or two for a deed?
faqs.a: Two. The county wants one check for the recording fee and a second for the realty transfer tax, both payable to the Recorder of Deeds, each showing the account holder's address.

faqs.q: Who owes the transfer tax on a Montgomery County sale?
faqs.a: State law makes them jointly responsible. The sales contract normally sets who really pays, and the combined rate collected at the Norristown counter is 2 percent.

faqs.q: Why can't a trust deed go through e-recording in Montgomery County?
faqs.a: No. Deeds with a trust must be recorded by mail or in person, because electronic recordings are public at once. Mortgages in default and plans are also excluded.

faqs.q: What if my deed has no parcel number yet?
faqs.a: Contact the Montgomery County Board of Assessments, which is across the hall from the recorder in Norristown. Every document must carry a registered 12-digit parcel number before it can be recorded.
